source_title: Civilization #9: Aeschylus, Sophocles, and Euripides as Prophets of Democracy
summary: This tragedy lecture is already public support for Human Heart and the atlas root: Greek theater trains democratic consciousness, while tragedy makes democracy see hubris, revenge, grief, imperial violence, and the human heart before those forces govern the city blindly.

existing_lens_links.episode_phrase: The public read already links prophets of democracy, democratic mirror-work, and tragedy deciphering what makes humans human to the Human Heart anchor.
existing_lens_links.rationale: Human Heart owns the active mechanism: tragedy as civic heart-knowledge, where public forms make revenge, hubris, grief, power, and self-accusation visible before they break the city.

existing_lens_links.episode_phrase: The public read already links theater turning democracy from procedure into shared identity and theater awakening people to the atlas-root world-making-media anchor.
existing_lens_links.rationale: The atlas root owns this as a compact relation rather than a full concept page: public symbolic forms train perception, identity, self-distance, and democratic consciousness.

concept_extensions.proposed_addition: Already public: keep this source as the 2024 civic-tragedy layer where Aeschylus, Sophocles, and Euripides teach democracy to see power, revenge, justice, grief, hubris, empire, and self-accusation as human-heart problems.
concept_extensions.boundary_note: Human Heart owns tragedy when the active mechanism is inner moral structure made publicly visible. Poetry owns tragedy as moral formation through language and catharsis; Fictional Heroes owns character inhabitation; Strategy owns war only when material capacity or war-board logic is primary.

concept_extensions.proposed_addition: Already public: keep this source inside the atlas root's World-Making Media relation, where Greek theater trains democratic citizenship, civic self-distance, perspective switching, and the capacity to be awakened out of a favorite story.
concept_extensions.boundary_note: The atlas relation should remain compact. A standalone Greek Theater, Tragedy, or Democratic Consciousness page is not needed unless later source fan-in creates a separate reader-navigation problem.

concept_extensions.proposed_addition: Use this source only as background when Poetry next receives tragedy compression: it supplies the earlier Athenian public-theater institution behind the later Great Books claim that tragedy forms moral selves through hubris, epiphany, and catharsis.
concept_extensions.boundary_note: Poetry should not absorb the whole democracy-facing source. Its narrow use is tragedy as poetic moral infrastructure; Human Heart keeps the civic heart-knowledge mechanism.

chronology_notes.note: Dated 2024-10-17, this source is an earlier public-read formulation of Greek theater as democratic consciousness training before the 2024-11-05 Aristotle lecture broadens the sequence into Homer, tragedy, Plato, Aristotle, and liberal arts education.

Jiang dates Trojan Women to 415 BCE after Athens's 416 BCE attack on Melos, and reads Pericles's funeral oration as the respectable version that Euripides reimagines as a mother holding her son's head.

next_actions.action: No public Human Heart, atlas, Poetry, or Fictional Heroes append is needed now; the strongest tragedy-democracy and theater-consciousness mechanisms are already public with durable anchors and episode read links.

Do not create standalone Aeschylus, Sophocles, Euripides, Greek Theater, Tragedy, Prophets Of Democracy, Democratic Self-Reflection, Melos, Bacchae, or Mother Holding The Head pages from this source alone.

If future synthesis revisits Greek tragedy, compare this source with the Aristotle Greek-legacy source and the Great Books Poets and Prophets tragedy/catharsis source before deciding whether the atlas root relation remains enough or a concept-scoped review is needed.
